title: 1 Timothy

stories.title: 📜 1 Timothy 1
summaryBullets: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, (1:1).
To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. (1:2).
As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines (1:3).
or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith. (1:4).
The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. (1:5).
Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk. (1:6).
They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert. (1:7).
Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately. (1:8).

We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers, (1:9).
for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching (1:10).
that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted. (1:11).
I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service. (1:12).
I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy. (1:13).
And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. (1:14).
This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. (1:15).

But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. (1:16).
Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. (1:17).
Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight, (1:18).
holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith. (1:19).
Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme. (1:20).
crossRefs: Galatians 1:6-9: Warning against another gospel.
Romans 7:12: The law is holy and good.
1 Corinthians 5:5: Delivering to Satan for discipline.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁבֶר אֱמוּנָה (šeḇer ʾĕmûnāh, sense), Greek: ναυαγέω περὶ τὴν πίστιν (nauagéō perì tēn pístin, NT), Aramaic: טבַע אִתְחַסְדָא (ṭabaʿ ʾitḥasdā, sense)
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for total ruin; describes abandoning faith and conscience like a wrecked ship.

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹפֵר (sopher); Greek: γραμματεύς (grammateus)
Greek: Ἔφεσος (Ephesos)
translationNotes.note: A harbour city on the Aegean coast of what is now western Turkey, and the seat of the Roman governor of the province of Asia. Its temple of Artemis was counted one of the seven wonders of the world; Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century, gives it as 425 feet long and 225 wide with 127 columns sixty feet high (Natural History 36.21). The temple also worked as a bank and a place of legal asylum, and the silversmiths who sold miniature shrines started a riot over Paul (Acts 19:23-41). Paul had already spent about three years there (Acts 20:31).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀνδραποδιστής (andrapodistēs)
translationNotes.note: The word means the man who seizes a free person and sells him into slavery, the kidnapper at the head of the slave trade rather than the buyer at the end of it. The law of Moses made that a capital crime twice over: Exodus 21:16 and Deuteronomy 24:7 both sentence the man-stealer to death. Paul's list in 1:9-10 tracks the second half of the Ten Commandments, and this word sits where stealing does.

translationNotes.term: Where Paul's word arsenokoitai comes from
translationNotes.original: Greek (LXX) Leviticus 18:22: μετὰ ἄρσενος οὐ κοιμηθήσῃ κοίτην γυναικός - Greek (LXX) Leviticus 20:13: ὃς ἂν κοιμηθῇ μετὰ ἄρσενος κοίτην γυναικός - Greek: ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai), singular ἀρσενοκοίτης (arsenokoites)
translationNotes.note: Paul's word arsenokoitai, at 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10, means men who lie with males. Literally it is male-bedders: men who engage in sexual acts with other males. Koite is the ordinary Greek word for a bed and the standard term for sexual intercourse, which is how the New Testament itself uses it at Romans 13:13 and Hebrews 13:4. The word is a rare compound, and its two halves stand side by side in the Greek Old Testament of two verses: Leviticus 18:22 reads meta arsenos ou koimethese koiten gynaikos, and Leviticus 20:13 reads hos an koimethe meta arsenos koiten gynaikos, where arsenos and koiten are adjacent.

translationNotes.original: Greek: παρέδωκα τῷ Σατανᾷ (paredoka to Satana), 'I handed over to Satan'
translationNotes.note: Paul names two men at 1:20, Hymenaeus and Alexander, and says he handed them over to Satan so that they would be taught not to blaspheme; the stated aim is corrective. He describes the same action against a man at Corinth in 1 Corinthians 5:5. Hymenaeus is named again at 2 Timothy 2:17, where he is said to have wandered from the truth by claiming the resurrection had already happened. The verb is paradidomi, the same one Romans 1:24 uses of God giving people over.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul charges Timothy to oppose false teaching, use the law rightly, remember Paul’s example of mercy, and hold faith and conscience to avoid shipwreck.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Timothy 2
summaryBullets: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone— (2:1).
for kings and all those in authority— so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity. (2:2).
This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, (2:3).
who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. (2:4).
For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, (2:5).
who gave Himself as a ransom for all — the testimony that was given at just the right time. (2:6).
For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything. (2:7).
Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension. (2:8).
Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, (2:9).
but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God. (2:10).
A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness. (2:11).
I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. (2:12).
For Adam was formed first, and then Eve. (2:13).
And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression. (2:14).
Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control. (2:15).
crossRefs: 1 Timothy 1:3-7: The letter states its own occasion in its opening lines, that Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to stop certain men teaching false doctrine, men who want to be teachers of the law without understanding what they so confidently assert.

1 Timothy 5:11-15: Paul writes of younger widows in this same church who go from house to house as gossips and busybodies, 'discussing things they should not mention', and says some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
Acts 18:26: Priscilla and Aquila take Apollos aside and explain the way of God to him more accurately, with Priscilla named first and Apollos already teaching publicly in the synagogue.
Romans 16:1-2: Paul commends Phoebe, a diakonos of the church at Cenchrea, to the church at Rome and tells them to give her whatever she needs.
1 Corinthians 11:5: The same writer takes it for granted that women pray and prophesy in the assembly, and his instruction there concerns their heads rather than their speaking.
Genesis 3:13-16: The account 2:13-14 appeals to, where the woman says the serpent deceived her and the consequences are pronounced.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵלִיץ (mēlîṣ, sense), Greek: μεσίτης (mesítēs, NT), Aramaic: מתווכחא (metawwakḥā, sense)
translationNotes.note: One who intervenes between two parties; in the NT used uniquely for Christ as sole mediator between God and humans.

translationNotes.term: Prayers for kings and all those in authority
translationNotes.note: This was the loyalty question of the age. Two sacrifices a day were offered in the Jerusalem temple for Caesar and the Roman people, and Josephus records that when the temple officials refused to accept them any longer in AD 66, that refusal was the act that started the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.197, 2.409). Rome did not demand that you love the emperor, only that you sacrifice to him. Paul tells the assemblies to pray for rulers, which is a thing they could do without sacrificing to any of them.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας (epairontas hosious cheiras)
translationNotes.note: The normal posture for prayer in that world was standing upright with both hands raised and open, not kneeling with the hands folded, which is a much later western habit. Solomon prayed that way at the dedication of the temple, standing with his hands spread toward heaven (1 Kings 8:22), and the Psalms describe it repeatedly (Psalm 28:2, 63:4, 141:2). Greeks and Romans prayed with raised hands too, so Paul's point falls on 'holy', not on the posture.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀντίλυτρον (antilytron)
translationNotes.note: A lytron was the purchase price paid to get a captive or a slave out, the sum handed over to free a body. Antilytron sharpens it with the prefix anti-, a price paid in place of the one held, and this is the only place the word occurs in the New Testament. Jesus uses the plain form of it in Mark 10:45, 'to give His life as a ransom for many'.

The letter states its own occasion. Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrine, men who want to be teachers of the law and do not understand what they so confidently assert (1:3-7). He names Hymenaeus and Alexander as two he has handed over to Satan (1:20), warns of teachers who will prohibit marriage and forbid foods (4:1-3), and ends on men who trade in disputes about words and treat godliness as a means of gain (6:3-5). Chapter 5 adds younger widows in the same church going house to house as gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not, some of whom have already turned aside (5:11-15).

translationNotes.original: Greek: αὐθεντεῖν (authentein)
translationNotes.note: This verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. 1 Timothy 2:12 is its single appearance, so there is no second use by Paul or anyone else to compare it against. The ordinary New Testament noun for authority is exousia (ἐξουσία), and Paul's regular verb for leading or presiding is proistemi (προΐστημι), which he uses in this same letter of an overseer managing his household (3:4-5), of a deacon (3:12), and of elders who lead well (5:17). None of those words is the one he chose here.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἡσυχία (hesychia) - ἡσύχιος (hesychios)
translationNotes.note: The same root appears twice in this chapter. At 2:2 Paul prays that all believers may lead 'tranquil and quiet lives', which is the adjective hesychios, and at 2:11-12 the woman is to learn in hesychia and to remain in it. Paul uses the noun again at 2 Thessalonians 3:12, where people who are living undisciplined lives are commanded to work quietly and earn their own living.

Scripture names women teaching, prophesying, and judging. Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:26); Phoebe is a diakonos of the church at Cenchrea, the same Greek word rendered 'deacon' at 1 Timothy 3:8 and Philippians 1:1 (Romans 16:1-2); Euodia and Syntyche contended at Paul's side for the gospel (Philippians 4:2-3); Philip's four unmarried daughters prophesied (Acts 21:9); and Paul writes of women praying and prophesying in the assembly (1 Corinthians 11:5). In the Old Testament Deborah the prophetess was judging Israel and the people went up to her for judgment (Judges 4:4-5), and the king's officials went to Huldah the prophetess to get the word of the LORD (2 Kings 22:14-20). Titus 2:3-5 has older women training the younger.

translationNotes.original: Greek: σωθήσεται διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας (sothesetai dia tes teknogonias)
translationNotes.note: The Greek shifts number inside the verse and English cannot show it. 'Will be saved' is singular and carries straight on from 'the woman' of 2:14, while 'if they continue in faith, love, and holiness' is plural. Teknogonia is the plain word for bearing children and stands here with the definite article, 'the childbearing'; Paul uses the matching verb at 5:14, where he tells younger widows to marry and bear children.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul urges prayer for all, affirms Christ as sole mediator, gives instructions for men’s prayer and women’s conduct, grounding them in creation and fall order.

stories.title: 📜 1 Timothy 3
summaryBullets: This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task. (3:1).
An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, (3:2).
not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money. (3:3).
An overseer must manage his own household well and keep his children under control, with complete dignity. (3:4).
For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God? (3:5).
He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil. (3:6).
Furthermore, he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil. (3:7).
Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. (3:8).
They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. (3:9).
Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons. (3:10).
In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things. (3:11).
A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household. (3:12).
For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. (3:13).
Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things (3:14).
in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. (3:15).

By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory. (3:16).
crossRefs: Acts 20:28: Overseers to care for the church of God.
Philippians 1:1: Overseers and deacons addressed.
Ephesians 2:19-20: God’s household built on Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּקִיד (pāqîd, sense), Greek: ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, NT), Aramaic: אפיסקופא (episqopā)
translationNotes.note: Literally ‘watcher, supervisor’; early church role of leadership, also translated bishop.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְשָׁרֵת (mĕšārēt, sense), Greek: διάκονος (diákonos, NT), Aramaic: משמשנא (mshamšānā)
translationNotes.note: Servant or minister; refers to recognized role of service in the church.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָז הַחֲסִידוּת (rāz haḥăsîdūt, sense), Greek: τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον (to tēs eusebeías mystḗrion, NT), Aramaic: רזא דחסידותא (razā d-ḥasîdūṯā)
translationNotes.note: Confession summarizing Christ’s incarnation, vindication, proclamation, belief, and exaltation.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (mias gynaikos andra)
translationNotes.note: Word for word, 'a one-woman man'. Read it against the world it was written into: under Roman law a marriage ended whenever either party withdrew from it, with no court and no stated cause; concubinage was a recognised legal status alongside marriage; and a wealthy man's use of the slaves in his own house was not counted against him by Roman law or Roman opinion. Paul lays the same requirement on deacons in 3:12 and on elders in Titus 1:6, and the mirror of it, 'wife of one husband', is the enrolment test for widows in 1 Timothy 5:9.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul lists qualifications for overseers and deacons, describes the church as God’s household, and confesses the mystery of godliness centered in Christ.

stories.title: 🌿 1 Timothy 4
summaryBullets: Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons, (4:1).
influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron. (4:2).
They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. (4:3).
For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, (4:4).
because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. (4:5).
By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed. (4:6).
But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. (4:7).
For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come. (4:8).
This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance. (4:9).
To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe. (4:10).
Command and teach these things. (4:11).
Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. (4:12).
Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching. (4:13).
Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders. (4:14).
Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all. (4:15).
Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you. (4:16).
crossRefs: 2 Thessalonians 2:3: Apostasy before the day of the Lord.
Genesis 1:31: God saw all he made was very good.
Acts 20:28: Pay careful attention to yourselves and to the flock.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶרֶד (méred, sense), Greek: ἀποστασία (apostasía, NT), Aramaic: מרוד (marōd, sense)
translationNotes.note: Means rebellion, falling away, or departure; used here for leaving the faith to follow deceptive teachings.

translationNotes.original: Greek: καυστηριάζω (kaustēriazō)
translationNotes.note: From kauterion, the branding iron; the English word cauterize comes from the same root. Runaway slaves and condemned criminals were branded on the forehead or hand with a hot iron as a permanent mark that could not be argued with. Branded skin scars over and stops feeling anything, which is the whole point of the image: a conscience burnt until it registers nothing.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μῦθος (mythos) - Greek: γενεαλογία (genealogia)
translationNotes.note: Paul makes this same complaint five times across these three letters and pairs it with the law every time: 1 Timothy 1:4 and 4:7, Titus 1:14 and 3:9, and 2 Timothy 4:4. The teaching he is describing spun stories and family-line speculation out of the Old Testament records and then argued about them, which is why he calls it 'speculation rather than the stewardship of God's work' in 1:4.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀνάγνωσις (anagnōsis)
translationNotes.note: Reading here is a public act, not a private one. Books were hand-copied scrolls, expensive enough that ordinary households did not own any, so almost everyone met Scripture by hearing it read aloud. That was the fixed synagogue practice on the sabbath (Luke 4:16-20; Acts 13:15; Acts 15:21), and Paul's own letters were written to be read out to the gathered assembly (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul warns against apostasy through false ascetic teaching and charges Timothy to train in godliness, set an example, use his gift, and guard his teaching.

headings.text: A Good Servant of Jesus Christ

stories.title: 📜 1 Timothy 5
summaryBullets: Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, (5:1).
older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity. (5:2).
Honor the widows who are truly widows. (5:3).
But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God. (5:4).
The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers. (5:5).
But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive. (5:6).
Give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach. (5:7).
If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. (5:8).
A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, faithful to her husband, (5:9).
and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work. (5:10).
But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry, (5:11).
and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith. (5:12).
At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention. (5:13).
So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander. (5:14).
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan. (5:15).
If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need. (5:16).
Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. (5:17).
For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.” (5:18).
Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. (5:19).
But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin. (5:20).
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality. (5:21).
Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure. (5:22).
Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments. (5:23).
The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later. (5:24).
In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden. (5:25).
crossRefs: Leviticus 19:32: Rise in the presence of the aged and honour the face of an old man.
Acts 6:1-6: Widows are overlooked in the daily distribution, and seven men are appointed to handle it.
Deuteronomy 25:4: Do not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.
Luke 10:7: Jesus says the worker is worthy of his wages.
Deuteronomy 19:15: A charge stands only on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּבוֹד כָּפוּל (kāḇōd kāfūl, sense), Greek: διπλῆς τιμῆς (diplēs timēs, NT), Aramaic: יָקָרא תְּרֵין (yāqārā treyn, sense)
translationNotes.note: Phrase meaning both respect and material support; applied to elders who labor in preaching and teaching.

translationNotes.original: Greek: καταλεγέσθω (katalegesthō)
translationNotes.note: This is a register, not a figure of speech. The verb is the one used for entering a man's name on a military roll or a civic list, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. The assembly was feeding these women out of its own funds, so the list carried entry requirements: sixty years old at least, wife of one husband, and a record of raising children, housing strangers, washing the feet of the saints, and helping the afflicted (5:9-10). Acts 6:1-6 shows the same welfare arrangement running daily in Jerusalem, and 5:16 tells families to carry their own widows so the fund is not swamped.

translationNotes.term: Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 25:4, quoted word for word. Grain was threshed by spreading the cut stalks on a hard flat floor and driving oxen over them, often dragging a weighted sledge, until the kernels broke free of the husks. The animal walked on food for hours, and the law forbids tying its mouth shut while it worked. Paul uses the same verse to argue for paying preachers in 1 Corinthians 9:9-10, and pairs it here with the words of Jesus in Luke 10:7.

translationNotes.term: A little wine because of your stomach
translationNotes.original: Greek: οἶνος (oinos)
translationNotes.note: Ancient drinking water came from cisterns, wells, and open channels, and there was no way to test or treat it; bad water was a constant fact of city life. Wine cut with water was the ordinary table drink, and the mixing made the water safer to swallow. Greek physicians also prescribed particular wines for particular stomach complaints, and the Hippocratic writings discuss which wine suits which condition. Timothy had apparently been drinking water only, and Paul is giving him medical advice, not lifting a restriction.

stories.keyTakeaway: Timothy is instructed how to treat different groups in the church - elders, widows, and church leaders - with guidance on recognizing worthy widows, supporting family members, compensating hardworking elders, and handling accusations against leaders. He is also charged to maintain impartiality and personal integrity in applying these instructions.

stories.title: 📜 1 Timothy 6
summaryBullets: All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited. (6:1).

Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles. (6:2).
If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching, (6:3).
he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions, (6:4).
and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of gain. (6:5).
Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. (6:6).
For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. (6:7).
But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these. (6:8).
Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. (6:9).
For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows. (6:10).
But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. (6:11).
Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses. (6:12).
I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate: (6:13).
Keep this commandment without stain or reproach until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, (6:14).
which the blessed and only Sovereign One— the King of kings and Lord of lords— will bring about in His own time. (6:15).
He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen. (6:16).
Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy. (6:17).
Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, (6:18).
treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life. (6:19).
O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge,” (6:20).
which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all. (6:21).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ζυγός (zygos)
translationNotes.note: The yoke is the wooden beam laid across the necks of a plough team, so the picture is of a man harnessed like an animal. Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race: people entered it through capture in war, piracy, debt, being exposed as infants, or being born to a slave mother, and slaves worked as miners, cooks, doctors, tutors, and estate managers. What Paul addresses in 6:2 is the situation the assemblies actually created, where a slave and the man who legally owned him sat in the same room as brothers.

translationNotes.original: Greek: φιλαργυρία (philargyria)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'love of silver'. The sentence is commonly quoted wrong. Paul does not write that money is the root of all evil; the Greek has no article, so it reads that love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. Six verses later he tells the rich to keep their wealth and use it, being generous and ready to share (6:17-19), which would be nonsense if the money itself were the problem.

The Roman prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36, under Tiberius. He was based at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem with troops for the feasts, when crowds made trouble likely. In 1961 a limestone block was found reused in the theatre at Caesarea carrying his name and his title, prefect of Judea, which puts the man and the office in stone. The confession Paul points to is the exchange in John 18:33-37.

translationNotes.term: King of kings and Lord of lords
translationNotes.original: Greek: βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων (basileus tōn basileuontōn)
translationNotes.note: This was a real imperial title before it was a hymn line. Great kings who ruled over lesser kings used it: Nebuchadnezzar is called king of kings in Daniel 2:37 and Ezekiel 26:7, and Artaxerxes signs himself that way in Ezra 7:12. Deuteronomy 10:17 had already applied the pattern to God, 'God of gods and Lord of lords'. Paul is putting the highest title a man could claim where it belongs.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul instructs Timothy on proper conduct for slaves and masters, warns against false teachers who promote controversy and greed, and charges him to pursue righteousness while commanding the wealthy to be generous rather than arrogant. He emphasizes that godliness with contentment is gain, the love of money leads to ruin, and urges Timothy to guard the faith against false knowledge.

intro:
1 Timothy was written by Paul the apostle (1 Timothy 1:1), the first of the three "Pastoral Epistles" (along with 2 Timothy and Titus), addressed to Paul's young protégé Timothy who was overseeing the church at Ephesus. The letter was composed around AD 63-65, after Paul's release from his first Roman imprisonment (AD 62, the end of Acts) and before his second arrest and execution under Nero (c. AD 66-67). After his release Paul undertook what is sometimes called his fourth missionary journey, traveling through Crete (where he left Titus to organize the churches), to Ephesus (where he left Timothy with similar oversight responsibility), and on into Macedonia, from which he wrote 1 Timothy: "As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies" (1 Timothy 1:3-4). The likely place of writing is Philippi or another Macedonian city. Timothy was a half-Jewish, half-Greek native of Lystra in southern Galatia (Acts 16:1); his mother Eunice was a Jewish believer and his grandmother Lois was also a believer (2 Timothy 1:5: "I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you also"), while his father was a Greek who is never mentioned by name. Paul had met Timothy on his second missionary journey when he passed through Lystra around AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3), found him already well-regarded by the believers in Lystra and Iconium, circumcised him for the sake of his ministry among Jews (since his Jewish mother had not had him circumcised in deference to his Greek father), and added him to the missionary team. Timothy thereafter became Paul's most trusted helper, co-greeting six of Paul's other letters (2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, and Philemon), serving as Paul's envoy on multiple delicate missions, and finally being left in Ephesus to oversee the strategic church there. According to the Acts of Timothy (a 5th-century work preserving older traditions), Timothy became the first bishop of Ephesus and was martyred there around AD 97 during the reign of the emperor Nerva (AD 96-98); he was clubbed, dragged, and stoned to death by a pagan mob during the festival of Artemis (the Katagogion) after he confronted the idolatrous procession and preached the true faith. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the city of Ephesus in the early-to-mid 60s AD, where Timothy was overseeing the church that Paul had founded a decade earlier during the three years of his third missionary journey (Acts 19, c. AD 53-56). Ephesus was the largest city of Asia Minor, the political capital of the Roman province of Asia, the religious center of the cult of Artemis, and home to the Temple of Artemis (one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World). For background on the city itself, the Temple of Artemis, and Paul's earlier ministry there, see the introduction to Ephesians. By the time Paul wrote 1 Timothy, the Ephesian church had grown substantially and was under pressure from false teachers promoting what 1 Timothy calls "myths and endless genealogies" (1:4), forbidding marriage and certain foods (4:1-5), and a "knowledge falsely so-called" (6:20) that some traditional commentators have identified with early forms of the Gnostic teaching that would flourish in the second century. The Roman emperor was Nero (AD 54-68), in the middle years of his reign, before the great fire of Rome (AD 64) and the subsequent persecution of Christians that would lead to Paul's own martyrdom. The earlier favorable years of Nero's reign under the influence of his tutor Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus were giving way to the increasingly erratic and violent later years.

1 Timothy is the fifty-fourth book of the Christian Bible, the fifteenth book of the New Testament, and the tenth of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. It is the first of the three Pastoral Epistles, so named because they are written to individual pastoral leaders (Timothy and Titus) rather than to congregations and because they address the practical concerns of pastoral church leadership. The letter has six chapters. The earliest surviving manuscripts include Codex Sinaiticus (4th century) and Codex Alexandrinus (5th century AD); the Pastoral Epistles are not preserved in Papyrus 46 (whose surviving leaves end in 1 Thessalonians), suggesting they were transmitted in a separate scribal tradition initially. Several of 1 Timothy's passages have become foundational to Christian doctrine and church practice: 1 Timothy 1:15 ("The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost"); 1 Timothy 2:5 ("There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus"); 1 Timothy 3:1-13 lists the character qualifications for overseers (also called elders or bishops) and deacons, which remain the standard New Testament credentials for church leadership; 1 Timothy 4:1-5 warns of those who "in later times" will "depart from the faith" by following "deceitful spirits and teachings of demons"; 1 Timothy 6:10 ("the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils"); and 1 Timothy 6:12 ("Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called").
